title: Kindness to animals
hookLine: Francis preaches to the birds and calls them sisters; the Buddhist Metta Sutta wishes well to all beings; Jains sweep the path
tomorrow: a man hurled insults at the Buddha. what did he do with them?

lines: A DOG, A CAT, A PIGEON.
cards: A dog waiting by a door. A cat on a windowsill. A pigeon working the sidewalk for crumbs.
Easy to walk past. Francis of Assisi, the story goes, stopped.

In the Little Flowers, a collection of stories about him, he sees a great crowd of birds near the road, tells his companions to wait, and goes over to preach to them. He calls them his little sisters.

teach.b: Today's question: do animals count? Francis's answer was the sermon itself. You owe God much, he tells the birds: your freedom to fly, your feathers for clothing, rivers to drink from, food you never sowed or reaped.
The story says they stretched out their necks and stayed until he blessed them, then flew off singing.
Later, in his Canticle of the Creatures, he praised God through Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind and Sister Water.
That's the Franciscan teaching: creatures are family, brothers and sisters made by one Creator, and caring for them is part of praise. Now a neighbor who shares it, in its own words.
The Buddhist Metta Sutta sends goodwill to every living being, weak or strong, great or small, seen or unseen, near or far, and wishes: may all beings be happy.
It asks for a heart toward all of them like a mother's toward her only child. And the first precept of Buddhist life is to refrain from taking life.

Jain monks and nuns carry their own vow of non-harm into every step, with a soft broom to clear tiny creatures from their path. Shared: animals stand inside the circle of care, not outside it. One honest difference.
Francis calls them siblings because one God made them, and his care is praise.
The Metta Sutta names no creator.
It wishes well to every being, simply because each one is a being.

how: Some churches bless animals around the feast of Saint Francis, and his Canticle of the Creatures is sung. Buddhists recite the Metta Sutta and keep the precept against taking life; Jain monks and nuns sweep their path to spare small creatures.

o: creatures inside your circle of care
a rule about which foods to avoid
only caring for the pets you own

p: preached to his little sisters, the birds

s: Francis preaching to the birds is a modern legend, not an old story
the Little Flowers of St. Francis tells it: the birds stayed until he blessed them.
the Metta Sutta wishes well to beings seen and unseen, near and far
it names the weak and strong, great and small, seen and unseen.
Francis and the Metta Sutta give the same reason for caring
Francis calls creatures siblings under one Creator; the Metta Sutta names no creator.

games.q: a wasp is stuck against your kitchen window. your roommate reaches for the spray. which choice fits both Francis and the Metta Sutta?
o: trap it under a glass and let it out the window
spray it; something that small doesn't really count
leave the room and hope it finds its own way out
games.why: both put small creatures inside the circle of care. the Metta Sutta names the small along with the great.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one animal you saw this week: a bird, a dog, a squirrel on a wire. Hold it the way the Metta Sutta asks, wishing it safety and ease. Stay with that one creature until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Kindness to animals: for Francis, care for creatures as brothers and sisters; in the Metta Sutta, goodwill toward every being.

orig.note: Pali: loving-kindness, the goodwill the Metta Sutta sends to all beings.

carryVoice: Carry this: all creatures, from the birds Francis called sisters to the smallest being in the Buddha's wish. Go gently.
